narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with not passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 35 was the second most important factor. While this score pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, it was not enough to overcome the much larger negative effect of your class rankings. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 worked in the same direction as your LSAT, modestly encouraging a pass prediction, but again its influence was smaller than the impact of your school performance.

In short, the model concluded that your relatively low standing within your law school classes outweighed your test scores and made success on the bar exam less likely.

What you should do next is focus on improving your class rank in the remaining part of your program if possible, or consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score significantly. Strengthening either area would likely change the prediction in your favor for future applications.
